design_detail: Pooled analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover phase I studies run in one laboratory at the University Hospital Basel: seven studies of 16 people each who took 125 mg MDMA twice, once alone and once after a pretreatment medicine (112 people); one unpublished study of 24 people who took 125 mg once; and one study of 30 people who took 75 mg once. At least seven days separated sessions. Only the sessions of MDMA alone against placebo are analysed in the paper (166 MDMA sessions); the 112 pretreatment sessions are in a supplement. Analysis: repeated-measures analyses of variance with drug (MDMA against placebo, within person), dose (75 against 125 mg, between people) and sex; Fisher's exact tests for the share of people crossing a clinical line; paired t tests of kidney, liver and blood-count tests at screening against an end-of-study visit. The two doses were given in different studies to different people, so the 75 against 125 mg contrast is between studies and was not randomised.
can_establish: What one oral dose of MDMA did, against placebo in the same people, to blood pressure, heart rate, ear temperature, self-rated drug effects and complaints in 166 healthy young adults sitting at rest in a hospital research unit with a research assistant present; how many of them crossed common clinical lines (systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 a minute, temperature above 38 degrees Celsius); and that creatinine, estimated kidney filtration and liver enzymes were unchanged on average about a month later. It also records how 141 of the 166 rated the overall experience, and whether they would consider taking MDMA again, when asked at the end of the study.
cannot_establish: What happens when people dance, are in a hot or crowded place, drink little or a lot, take other drugs, take pills of unknown content or take further doses (all absent by design); risks in people with heart disease or mental health conditions (excluded); how often rare events (under 1 in 100) such as a temperature above 40 degrees Celsius occur (the authors' own calculation allows up to 1.3% for no event in 278 sessions); anything about blood sodium (not measured); changes in the kidney in the hours and days after a dose (blood was taken about a month later); and a dose-response for temperature or heart rate that is not mixed up with differences between studies. Why people take MDMA or what they seek from it: the volunteers did not choose the dose or the setting, four in five were new to MDMA, and their answers about taking it again come after one or two hospital sessions.

sample.recruitment: Mostly recruited from the University of Basel campus and paid for taking part (Methods > Subjects, 1st paragraph, p. 577; Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph, p. 577).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy European or Caucasian adults aged 18-45, psychiatrically screened. Excluded: a history of psychiatric disorder or physical illness, illicit drug use on more than five occasions in a lifetime (past cannabis use allowed), illicit drug use in the past two months or during the study (urine tests before sessions); the detailed criteria are in the earlier papers of each study (Methods > Subjects, 1st-2nd paragraphs, p. 577).
sample.demographics: Age 24.5 (SD 4) years, body weight 69 (SD 10) kg (range 46-95), equal numbers of women and men (83 each). 59 people had used a drug 1-5 times before, of whom 34 had used MDMA 1-4 times; 80% were MDMA-naive (Methods > Subjects, p. 577; Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph, p. 582).
sample.attrition: Not described for the pooled sample. Two people lacked kidney and liver tests and five lacked blood counts at the end-of-study visit (Table 4 footnotes, p. 583); four people reported no subjective effect and were left out of the timing analysis (Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph, p. 578); 141 of 166 answered the end-of-study questions (Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit, p. 578).
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy, paid volunteers, screened for illness and drug use, mostly new to MDMA. People with heart disease or psychiatric illness are absent by design, and the authors say so (Discussion > limitations paragraph, p. 585). A sample chosen to be healthy cannot show who is more at risk.

exposure.measurement: Dose given by the study team as gelatin capsules of MDMA hydrochloride from a pharmaceutical supplier; peak plasma MDMA and the area under the curve to 6 hours were measured in every person (Methods > Study drug, pp. 577-578; Methods > Plasma concentrations of MDMA, p. 578; Table 1, p. 581).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral MDMA 75 mg (30 people) or 125 mg (136 people), once or, in 112 people, twice at least seven days apart (once alone, once after a pretreatment medicine). Doses were not adjusted for weight: dose per body weight averaged 1.7 (SD 0.4) mg/kg overall, with 125 mg working out at 1.7 (SD 0.2) in men and 2.1 (SD 0.3) in women (Methods > Study drug, p. 578).
exposure.polysubstance: No illicit drug use in the two months before or during the study, checked by urine tests before sessions; the sessions with a pretreatment medicine are excluded from the main analysis (Methods > Subjects, 2nd paragraph, p. 577; Methods > Study design, p. 577).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least two months free of illicit drugs by history, with a urine screen before each session; at least seven days between sessions (Methods > Study design and Subjects, p. 577).

comparison.controls: Placebo session in each study, in the same people (double-blind crossover). For the dose comparison, the 30 people given 75 mg and the 136 given 125 mg are different people in different studies.
comparison.matching: Within-person for MDMA against placebo. Between the dose groups there is no matching and no randomisation; the paper does not report whether the order of sessions was randomised or counterbalanced in each study (the original reports hold that).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for MDMA against placebo, which is within person. For the dose comparison, differences between the studies are unmeasured: the placebo sessions of the 75 mg study averaged a highest ear temperature of 37.0 degrees Celsius and those of the 125 mg studies 37.4 (Table 2, p. 582), and the 75 mg study lacked two temperature time points.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded by screening and urine tests.

outcomes.instruments: Blood pressure and heart rate by automatic oscillometric device, in duplicate one minute apart after at least 10 minutes' rest; core (ear, tympanic) temperature by a two-ear infrared thermometer; each at 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours; visual analogue scales for any, good and bad drug effect; the 66-item List of Complaints at 3-6 and 24 hours; adverse events from 24 hours to 14 days; kidney and liver tests (creatinine, Cockcroft-Gault estimated filtration, enzymes) and blood counts at screening and an end-of-study visit; an end-of-study questionnaire (Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, p. 578; Blood sampling and EOS visit, p. 578).
outcomes.validity_norms: Clinical thresholds: systolic pressure above 140, 160 and 180 mm Hg and diastolic above 90, 100 and 110 for grades I-III of hypertension, heart rate above 100 a minute for tachycardia, temperature above 38 and 40 degrees Celsius for hyperthermia and hyperpyrexia (Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 3rd paragraph, p. 578). Ear temperature is a convenient, not a reference, measure of core temperature; the paper does not discuss its accuracy.
outcomes.operationalization: Table 2 takes each person's highest value in the 6 hours and reports the average of these highest values and the number of people whose highest value crossed each line, so the shares are shares of people who crossed a line at least once. The more readings are taken, the likelier one crosses a line.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated for the many comparisons (editors' count of 60: Table 1, 8; Table 2, 15; Table 3, 28 complaint comparisons; Table 4, 9 blood tests); Tukey post hoc tests followed significant analysis-of-variance effects; significance was set at p<0.05 throughout (Methods > Statistical analyses, p. 578).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind in design. The paper does not report whether people or staff could tell MDMA from placebo, which with 125 mg is likely. Blood pressure, pulse and temperature are device readings; drug effects and complaints are self-ratings.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2 (p. 582), average of each person's highest value, MDMA against placebo. 125 mg (n=136): systolic 157 (SD 15) against 133 (15) mm Hg; diastolic 93 (10) against 79 (8); heart rate 95 (17) against 76 (12) beats a minute; temperature 37.7 (0.5) against 37.4 (0.5) degrees Celsius. People above each line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 51 (38%) against 8 (6%); >180 7 (5%) against 0; heart rate >100 45 (33%) against 3 (2%); temperature >38 32 (24%) against 12 (9%). Highest single values 196 against 175 mm Hg systolic, 145 against 117 beats a minute, 39.1 against 38.7 degrees. 75 mg (n=30): systolic 145 (14) against 131 (11); diastolic 84 (8) against 77 (5); heart rate 83 (17) against 69 (9); temperature 37.2 (0.3) against 37.0 (0.3); above the lines: systolic >160 3 (10%) against 0; heart rate >100 3 (10%) against 0; temperature >38 0 against 0. Over all 166: systolic >160 in 54 (33%), >180 in 7 (4%), heart rate >100 in 48 (29%), temperature >38 in 32 (19%), highest 39.1 degrees; no temperature above 40 and no hypertensive urgency (Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, p. 580). Drug effect on every vital sign F >44, p<0.001; drug-by-dose interaction significant for systolic (F 15.2) and diastolic (F 17.9) pressure and not for heart rate (F 2.38) or temperature (F 2.43). Editors' calculation: at 125 mg, extra people above the line with MDMA against placebo 32 in 100 for systolic >160, 31 in 100 for heart rate >100 and 15 in 100 for temperature >38.
analysis.covariates: Sex and dose as factors; dose per body weight and peak plasma MDMA entered as covariates to test whether sex differences were due to dose per kilogram or blood level (Methods > Statistical analyses, p. 578).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Each of the nine studies is listed with a ClinicalTrials.gov number (NCT00886886, NCT00990067, NCT01136278, NCT01270672, NCT01386177, NCT01465685, NCT01771874, NCT01951508, NCT01616407); the pooled safety analysis is not described as preregistered (Methods > Study design, p. 577).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives the shares above each line for MDMA only, without the 9% of placebo sessions at 125 mg that also crossed 38 degrees Celsius, and says all three shares were greater at 125 than at 75 mg, while the dose-by-drug tests for heart rate and temperature are not significant. The pretreatment sessions are in a supplement that was not read. About 60 outcomes were tested without correction.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors call 166 a large sample next to earlier laboratory studies of 6-30 people, and state that it cannot rule out events at 0.1-1% or below; for no temperature above 40 degrees in 278 sessions the binomial upper bound is 1.3% (Introduction, p. 577; Discussion > limitations paragraph, p. 585).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 166 healthy volunteers sitting in a laboratory at about 22.7 degrees Celsius, a single dose of 75 or 125 mg raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo. At 125 mg, 38 in 100 reached a systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg (6 in 100 on placebo), 33 in 100 a heart rate above 100 (2 in 100) and 24 in 100 a temperature above 38 degrees (9 in 100); the highest values were 196 mm Hg and 39.1 degrees, with no hypertensive urgency and no temperature above 40. Dry mouth, loss of appetite, trouble concentrating, sweating and jaw clenching were common; creatinine, estimated filtration and liver enzymes did not change on average at about a month; women gave higher bad-drug-effect ratings and reported more complaints. Blood sodium was not measured. Asked at the end of the study, 95 of 141 volunteers (67%) called the overall experience positive, 25 (18%) neutral and 21 (15%) disappointing or bad.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusion say MDMA was overall safe in physically and psychiatrically healthy subjects in a medical setting, that all three shares above the lines were significantly greater at 125 than at 75 mg, and that risks are likely higher in people with cardiovascular disease. The Conclusion also recommends a fixed dose for women; that recommendation rests on comparing different studies (30 against 136 people) and is not reproduced here. The Discussion also says the study showed clearly greater positive than negative acute subjective effects, that psychological distress was minimal and that there were no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks; no measure of distress other than the 'bad drug effect' rating and the one-item anxiety complaint is reported.

timeline.event: Earlier analysis of laboratory studies in 74 volunteers from the same group (Liechti et al.), as cited by these authors: systolic pressure at or above 160 mm Hg in 32% and at or above 180 in 9%.

An independent laboratory (Freedman et al.), as summarized in a narrative review: core temperature up 0.4 and 0.6 degrees Celsius in a cool and a warm room, in 10 volunteers given a weight-based dose.
An independent laboratory (Kolbrich et al.), as summarized in the same review: ear temperature up on average 0.3-0.4 degrees in 8 volunteers, not significant, with one person up 1.9.
Parrott's review gathers the human temperature studies and finds a dose-related rise in laboratory studies

replication.where_it_stands: A rise in blood pressure, heart rate and temperature after a single dose at rest is seen in this laboratory's nine studies and, as summarized second-hand in a review, by independent laboratories. The nine studies share site, team and methods, so they are one team's replication. The shares above each line for 75 against 125 mg rest on this paper alone.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation (grants 323230_126231, 32323B_144996 and 320030_149493) (Funding, p. 586).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared (Declaration of conflicting interests, p. 586).
funding.affiliations_note: University Hospital Basel and University of Basel; all nine studies come from the senior author's laboratory, which also ran the studies behind most of the papers it cites for comparison.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person comparison of two or more doses, order randomised, with every temperature taken at the same time points by the same method and a warm-room condition, plus blood sodium, creatinine and a muscle enzyme measured in the first day after dosing, and a sample that includes older people and people with a raised blood pressure at the start.

domains.note: Described as double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover; the sequence generation and any counterbalancing are not described in this paper and no period effect is reported.
At least seven days between sessions, which the authors judge enough to exclude carry-over.
With 125 mg and a 4-hour drug effect, blinding probably did not hold, and no check is reported; the main outcomes are device readings, which expectation affects little.

The 75 mg study lacks temperature at 0.33 and 2.5 hours and one 125 mg study (24 people) lacks it at 2 hours; the highest temperature came on average at 2.4 hours (SD 1.2), so a person's true peak may be missed, more often in the 75 mg group.

Ear temperature is an indirect measure; placebo sessions averaged 37.0 degrees in the 75 mg study and 37.4 in the 125 mg studies, and 9% of placebo sessions at 125 mg crossed 38 degrees, so the line is crossed by chance and by measurement.

The pooled analysis was not preregistered; about 60 outcomes were tested without correction; the abstract features threshold shares that favour a dose effect which the continuous tests for heart rate and temperature do not show.

domains.domain: Dose comparison, 75 against 125 mg (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Different people in different studies, not randomised, with different time points and placebo temperatures; every dose-response statement in the paper rests on this contrast.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The comparison of MDMA with placebo in the same people (the first six rows) is at some concerns at worst, and its effects on blood pressure and pulse are large (F 292-486) next to the sources of bias named. The overall judgment is set by the dose comparison, which is between studies and was not randomised. The source can be cited for what a single dose of 125 mg did to blood pressure, pulse and ear temperature against placebo in healthy volunteers at rest, for the highest values seen, and for unchanged kidney and liver tests about a month later; it should not be cited for how temperature or heart rate change between 75 and 125 mg, for settings with heat, activity or crowding, or for people who are not healthy.

key_findings.finding: Nine double-blind placebo-controlled crossover studies from one hospital in Basel were pooled: 166 healthy volunteers (83 women, 83 men), 75 mg in 30 people and 125 mg in 136; aged 18-45; 80% new to MDMA. Room temperature averaged 22.7 degrees Celsius (SD 0.6) and a research assistant was always present.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Study design and Subjects (p. 577); Figure 1 legend (p. 579); Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (p. 580); Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (p. 582); Discussion > paragraph beginning 'The present safety data' (p. 585)

key_findings.finding: MDMA alone raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo. Of the 166, 54 (33%) reached a systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg and 7 (4%) above 180; 48 (29%) a heart rate above 100 a minute; 32 (19%) a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, up to 39.1. There was no hypertensive urgency and no temperature above 40; the highest systolic and diastolic pressures were 196 and 130 mm Hg.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (left column to the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: At 125 mg (n=136) the average of each person's highest reading was 157 mm Hg systolic (placebo 133), 93 diastolic (79), 95 beats a minute (76) and 37.7 degrees Celsius (37.4). The share above each line was 38% against 6% on placebo for systolic >160, 33% against 2% for heart rate >100 and 24% against 9% for temperature >38.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, right-hand block (125 mg, n=136)

key_findings.finding: At 75 mg (n=30) the averages were 145 mm Hg systolic (placebo 131), 84 diastolic (77), 83 beats a minute (69) and 37.2 degrees Celsius (37.0); 3 people (10%) went above 160 systolic and 3 (10%) above 100 beats a minute, against none on placebo, and nobody was above 38 degrees on MDMA or on placebo.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, left-hand block (75 mg, n=30)

key_findings.finding: Dose comparison: the drug-by-dose test was significant for systolic and diastolic pressure (F 15.2 and 17.9, p<0.001) but not for heart rate (F 2.38) or temperature (F 2.43); the shares above the lines were higher at 125 than at 75 mg (systolic >160 p<0.01, heart rate >100 p<0.05, temperature >38 p<0.01). The doses were given in different studies to different people.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (p. 580); Table 2, columns 'Drug x dose' (p. 582)

key_findings.finding: Timing: effects began on average 33 minutes (SD 24) after the dose, peaked at 1.6 hours (SD 0.8) and lasted 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4-8.2), with no difference in duration by dose or sex; the highest systolic pressure came at 1.7 hours (SD 0.9), the highest heart rate at 2.0 (SD 1.4) and the highest temperature at 2.4 (SD 1.2).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph; Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ratings of any and good drug effect were higher at 125 than at 75 mg (good drug effect, highest rating out of 100, average: women 82 against 60, men 77 against 57); bad drug effect was not dose-dependent and was higher in women (24 at 125 mg and 35 at 75 mg) than in men (13 and 7). Four of the 166 reported no subjective effect at all and were left out of the timing analysis; the paper does not say which dose they had or what their blood pressure, pulse or temperature did.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph (p. 578); Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA (p. 580); Table 1 (p. 581)

key_findings.finding: Peak blood MDMA was on average 1.8 times higher after 125 than after 75 mg (224.1 against 124.5 ng/mL), more than the 1.67-fold dose increase, significant in women only; at 125 mg women had about 1.3 times the peak level of men.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Cmax rows (p. 581); Results > Plasma concentrations of MDMA (p. 582)

key_findings.finding: Sex: no overall sex difference in vital signs; after allowing for the lower dose per kilogram in men, men showed the bigger rise in systolic pressure (F 6.08, p<0.05). Women reported more complaints (acute rise 8.8 against 6.4 points; the day after 5.4 against 3.0).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph; Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Most frequent acute complaints with MDMA (of 166), against placebo: lack of appetite 59%, dry mouth 55%, difficulty concentrating 46%, cold feet 42%, sweating 41%, jaw clenching 40% (of 134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, palpitations 24%; no serious adverse event occurred.
key_findings.locator: Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 2nd paragraph (p. 580); Table 3 (p. 583)

key_findings.finding: Kidney and liver tests at screening against the end-of-study visit (29 days on average after the last dose, SD 22; 164 people): creatinine 74 (SD 13) against 73 (12) micromoles a litre, estimated filtration 122 (22) against 125 (24) mL a minute, neither significantly changed; liver enzymes AST and ALT unchanged; GGT 19 against 18 U/L (p<0.01). Red cells and haemoglobin fell and platelets rose, which the authors put down to 400-600 mL of blood taken for analysis.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit (p. 578); Results > Effects of MDMA on kidney and liver function, 1st paragraph (p. 582); Table 4 (p. 583); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In the present study, MDMA did not influence' (p. 585)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that no controlled clinical study of MDMA has reported hyperpyrexia (above 40 degrees Celsius), possibly because participants took moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded environment, unlike some recreational settings. This is their suggestion, not a tested result.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Acute tolerance: the authors argue that subjective effects fall although blood MDMA stays high, so that adding more MDMA might not lengthen the effect and may add adverse effects; in their data the duration at 75 and 125 mg did not differ. This is an interpretation citing other studies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: kidney and liver tests only about a month later (short-lasting changes not excluded); sodium low after MDMA, which is frequently seen in intoxications, was not assessed; 278 sessions are too few to exclude events at 0.1-1% (no temperature above 40 degrees, binomial upper bound 1.3%); only healthy young people, and older people with cardiovascular risk factors may be treated in future.
key_findings.locator: Discussion > limitations paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Highest self-rating after the dose (Emax on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD)), MDMA against placebo. Any drug effect: 125 mg women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); 75 mg women 59 (29) against 3 (6), men 56 (32) against 6 (9). Good drug effect: 125 mg women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); 75 mg women 60 (28) against 6 (13), men 57 (33) against 7 (12). Bad drug effect: 125 mg women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); 75 mg women 35 (33) against 4 (13), men 7 (11) against 6 (16). Groups: 68 women and 68 men at 125 mg, 15 and 15 at 75 mg; drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44, p < 0.001 (the 125 and 75 mg groups are different people in different studies).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows 'Any drug effect', 'Good drug effect' and 'Bad drug effect'; Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 580)
key_findings.note: Read on a rendered image of the printed page; the means for men and women at each dose are as printed.

key_findings.finding: Tests on the self-ratings (F(1,162)): drug-by-dose for any drug effect F 20 (p < 0.001), good drug effect F 20 (printed p < 0.01) and bad drug effect F 0.001 (not significant); drug-by-sex for any drug effect F 3.4 (p = 0.068), good drug effect F 0.9 (not significant) and bad drug effect F 16 (p < 0.001); drug-by-dose-by-sex for bad drug effect F 3.6 (p = 0.059). Women gave higher bad-drug-effect ratings after MDMA than men, also after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0, p < 0.001) and for blood MDMA level (F 21.5, p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns 'Drug x dose', 'Drug x sex' and 'Drug x dose x sex' (p. 581); Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 580)

key_findings.finding: Complaints on the List of Complaints up to 6 hours after the dose, MDMA against placebo, n (%) of 166: lack of appetite 98 (59%) against 3 (2%); dry mouth 91 (55%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 76 (46%) against 10 (6%); cold feet 69 (42%) against 7 (4%); sweating 68 (41%) against 0; jaw clenching 54 (40%, of 134 asked) against 1 (1%); restless legs 62 (37%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 57 (34%) against 2 (1%); hot flushes 52 (31%) against 0; heart palpitations 40 (24%) against 2 (1%); lack of energy 38 (23%) against 23 (14%); nausea 19 (11%) against 2 (1%); anxiety 9 (6%) against 0; headache 42 (25%) against 27 (16%, not significantly different). Both doses (75 and 125 mg) are pooled in this table.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, columns 'Acute, up to 6 h' (placebo and MDMA)
key_findings.note: Read on a rendered image of the printed page. The complaints were rated 3 to 6 hours after the dose for the period up to 6 hours.

key_findings.finding: Complaints 24 hours after the dose, MDMA against placebo, n (%) of 166: lack of appetite 52 (31%) against 1 (1%); dry mouth 37 (23%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 35 (22%) against 4 (2%); headache 55 (33%) against 25 (15%); lack of energy 49 (30%) against 5 (3%); jaw clenching 19 (14%) against 1 (1%); hot flushes 12 (7%) against 0; restless legs 12 (7%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 12 (7%) against 3 (2%); heart palpitations 11 (7%) against 1 (1%); cold feet 10 (6%) against 2 (1%); nausea 9 (6%) against 1 (1%); sweating 7 (4%) against 0; anxiety 3 (2%) against 0 (not significant). The authors name headache, lack of energy and lack of appetite as the most frequent at 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, columns 'Subacute, 24 h' (p. 583); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: No serious adverse event occurred. Acute anxiety on the List of Complaints was reported by 9 people (6%) after 125 mg and none after 75 mg. Adverse events reported from 24 hours to 7 to 14 days included depressed mood in 4% after 125 mg MDMA (none listed after placebo or 75 mg) and headache in 6% after 125 mg, 7% after 75 mg and 5% after placebo; none was reported significantly more often after MDMA than after placebo. In the studies using 125 mg, 12 people (9%) reported 'flashbacks' (not defined in the paper) 1 to 3 times, one of them eight times, on average 26 hours (SD 15; range 8 to 50) after the dose; no sex differences; of 141 asked at the end of the study, 12 (9%) reported them, all within 8 to 50 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 2nd paragraph (p. 580, continued on p. 582); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: Asked at the end of the study (141 of the 166 volunteers; 80% new to MDMA, the rest with at most four earlier exposures): 95 (67%) reported a positive overall experience, 25 (18%) neutral and 21 (15%) disappointing or bad, with no sex differences. Would they consider taking MDMA again: 27 (19%) probably not under any circumstances; 66 (47%) not recreationally but possibly in another controlled study; 48 (34%) possibly in a recreational setting but only if identity, purity and dose were known, of whom 24 had earlier taken illicit drugs including MDMA; only 13 considered a club setting. The controlled setting had no impact on the experience for 51 (36%) and was important for the type of experience, reassuring and made them feel safe for 90 (64%); women rated the setting as more important (F(1,139) 12.4, p < 0.001). Their retrospective rating of the duration of the effect was 4.0 hours (SD 2.9).
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (pp. 582 to 584); Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 580)
key_findings.note: Volunteers were given MDMA by researchers; the 25 not asked are not explained.

key_findings.finding: The authors read the data as showing clearly greater positive than negative acute subjective effects and a state of predominantly positive mood across laboratories, with modest apprehension anxiety in some volunteers, no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks and minimal psychological distress; they contrast this with panic attacks and agitation or aggression described in people who use ecstasy and present to emergency departments (cited from other papers, not read).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that similar amounts of MDMA are found in ecstasy pills (citing Brunt et al. 2012, not read) and are used in clinical studies in patients; the capsules were pharmaceutical MDMA hydrochloride of known amount.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand comparison with pill content; no pill analysis was done in this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 19% of subjects above 38 degrees Celsius with MDMA and 33% and 29% above the blood pressure and heart rate lines, without the placebo shares. Table 2 shows that at 125 mg 12 of 136 placebo sessions (9%) also crossed 38 degrees, 8 (6%) crossed 160 mm Hg systolic and 3 (2%) crossed 100 beats a minute.
reporting_issues.consequence: The excess caused by MDMA at 125 mg is smaller than the headline for temperature: 24% against 9%, about 15 in 100 more (editors' calculation), and the temperature line is partly crossed by chance and by measurement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the shares with raised blood pressure, fast pulse and temperature above 38 degrees were all significantly greater at 125 than at 75 mg. The continuous dose-by-drug tests for heart rate (F 2.38) and temperature (F 2.43) are not significant, 0 of 30 people at 75 mg crossed 38 degrees against 24% at 125 mg, the 75 mg study lacks temperature readings at 0.33 and 2.5 hours, and the placebo sessions of the two doses differ (37.0 against 37.4 degrees on average).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose contrast for temperature and heart rate is between studies and partly an artefact of readings and baseline; it should not be quoted as a dose-response for those two measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says liver enzymes were similar at screening and at the end-of-study visit, but Table 4 shows GGT 19 (SD 8) against 18 (SD 8) U/L with t=2.73, p<0.01. The interval from the last dose to the end-of-study visit is 29 (SD 22) days in the Methods and 30 (SD 22) in the Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: The GGT change is statistically significant and clinically trivial; the text and table disagree, and the interval is stated two ways.

reporting_issues.issue: Acute anxiety is given as 9 people (6%) after 125 mg in the Results and Table 3 (9 of 166 is 5%), and as 7% in the Discussion (9 of 136 is 7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small slip in a percentage; the count of 9 is consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods sentence that defines the blood pressure grades is garbled (the thresholds are listed without saying which belong to systolic and diastolic readings in full); Table 2 shows that the thresholds used were systolic above 140, 160, 180 and diastolic above 90, 100, 110.
reporting_issues.consequence: Thresholds must be read from Table 2, not from the sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion recommends a fixed dose for women on the strength of a comparison between 15 women given 75 mg in one study and 68 given 125 mg in other studies, with bad-drug-effect ratings not dose-dependent.
reporting_issues.consequence: A recommendation about amounts that the between-study design cannot support; not reproduced in any claim.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the drug-by-dose test for 'any drug effect' and for 'good drug effect' is printed with the same F (20) but p < 0.001 for the first and p < 0.01 for the second; F(1,162) = 20 gives p of about 0.00001 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: A printing slip; the dose effect on the good-effect rating is stronger than printed. The two doses were given to different people in different studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The end-of-study questions (overall experience, interest in taking MDMA again, setting) were put to 141 of the 166 volunteers; the 25 who were not asked are not explained, and the answers come from people given MDMA by researchers, 80% of them new to it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The shares calling the experience positive (67%) or disappointing or bad (15%) are shares of volunteers, not of people who choose to take MDMA, and may differ for the 25 not asked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says psychological distress was minimal and that there were no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks, but the Results report no distress scale: the only measures are the 'bad drug effect' rating (mean 7 to 35 out of 100 across the four groups, with SDs of 11 to 33, so some volunteers rated it much higher) and the one-item anxiety complaint (6%); no distribution or highest value is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not say what the statements rest on beyond those two items; how high the highest bad-drug-effect ratings went is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The end-of-study visit, where the overall-experience and interest-in-taking-MDMA-again questions were put, took place on average 29 days (SD 22) after the last MDMA dose and after one or two doses; 112 of the 166 volunteers received 125 mg twice, once alone and once after a pretreatment medicine. The paper does not say which session the answers refer to.
reporting_issues.consequence: The shares calling the experience positive (67%) or disappointing or bad (15%) could describe the first session, the last or both together, and for 112 volunteers one of the two sessions followed another drug; they are a summary given weeks later, not ratings taken during a session.

reporting_issues.issue: Five of the 84 percentages in Table 3 are one point above the count over its group when rounded in the usual way (editors' calculation): acute anxiety 9 people printed as 6% (5.4% of 166), 24-hour dry mouth 37 as 23% (22.3%), 24-hour difficulty concentrating 35 as 22% (21.1%), 24-hour nausea 9 as 6% (5.4%) and placebo bruxism at 0 h 2 of 134 as 2% (1.5%). The Results give acute anxiety as 9 people (6%) 'after the 125 mg dose' and the Discussion as 7% after 125 mg (9 of 136 is 6.6%).
reporting_issues.consequence: A rounding slip of one point in a few cells; the counts are the same in all three places (9 people, all after 125 mg), and the printed share for anxiety depends on which group it is taken from.
